article.title: Progressive Activists Win Elections
article.author: Michael Albert
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Electoral effort powerfully trounced Trumpism. Not to death, but getting closer. Some election postmortem prescriptions inspire. Some disturb. Which is which? Large sectors of America want serious change. Perched a bit behind them, many other Americans are wavering. And next on the involvement spectrum, quite a few MAGA members are seriously shook up. What can now sustain the gains to go further? As with most social issues and possibilities, there are better and worse answers. Can we at least identify a dividing line? Can we even agree on what makes activist choices better or worse? Can we describe some specific choices of each sort? If so, perhaps we can use such criteria in context of our situations and preferences to choose tasks wisely. To see a dividing line is easy enough. Good choices communicate and act in ways that reveal the possibility of worthy sustainable change. They might bring MAGA-leaning and other system defenders out of system defense. They might bring cynics away from passivity. They might bring anger toward advocating change and bring inactive toward collective activity. In contrast, choices that urge, entice, or even unintentionally move people toward cynical system defense will be negative. Think of the population as people with diverse beliefs and habits that propel or inhibit their seeking new social relations. With that image in mind, good post-election choices will promote, attract, and welcome folks from various positions on the “involvement spectrum” toward the progressive, active end. Harmful post-election words and actions will entrench people far from activism or even move them into aggressive defense of existing relations. Is this explanatory picture too damn simple to help us? It doesn’t touch every base. It isn’t precise. But I think it’s more complex than it at first appears. For example, if your post-election words and deeds tend to move people out of MAGA is that more or less valuable than if your words and deeds move people from passivity toward progressive involvement, or from being somewhat active toward being more active? It depends not only on how much people moved, but are we talking about immediate or longer-term impact? Still, a shift toward progressive change from every position on the involvement spectrum will certainly be positive. Likewise, to shift people toward passivity or even toward defending or worsening the system from every position will certainly be negative. But the devil is in the details. Related: Beyond the Blue Wave: Why Winning Elections Isn't Enough Will any specific choice slide people one way or the other along the involvement spectrum? And of all the possible choices that push positively, which should we aid? Do we ask that question? Do we orient ourselves in part in light of our answers? Can we even assess what specifically moves people toward the progressive or even the radical or revolutionary end of the involvement spectrum? Or assess what instead moves people toward the reactionary, system-defending, cynically a-political, passive or even submissive end of the involvement spectrum? And to complicate assessments, don’t some choices move some people one way but other people the opposite way? We won’t all suddenly agree on the extent of the push-toward-activism or push away from activism effects of different choices on different people. So is one choice certainly right with all other choices certainly wrong? My first point is that no one should say to other activists do it my way or you are part of the problem. Do it my way or you are my enemy. That is a sectarian path that would squander current momentum. To instead respectfully consider and assess contending possibilities would likely be far more productive. But in that case, what options do people currently propose? Hold Trump and his sycophants accountable with public investigations, impeachments, and prosecutions. Prepare to win bigger ballot box gains in 2028 by working electorally with the Democratic Party as a whole or with particular preferred candidates even while opposing others. Urge, demand and organize to win universal free health care, an end to ICE and to the war with Iran and to weapons sales to Israel, restore public education, protect sexual and social diversity, restore cancelled government agencies, prosecute corruption, terminate tariff idiocy, reduce prices, lift low incomes, and enact a national wealth tax plus draconian consequences for trying to flee it. Use diverse words and tactics to accomplish each. Promote, urge, and organize new workplace, campus, and community organizations and grow existing ones. And develop and spread shared social vision, strategy, and program to orient institutional renovations and inspire sustained struggle beyond 2028. All four types of activity and their many possible diverse tactics and messages can slide involved activists, beneficiaries of the efforts, and even viewers of the efforts along the involvement spectrum. Done dismissively the drift could generate antagonism and even hostility more than it generates support. Done in ways that hear, welcome, and empower whoever the efforts encounter, the drift could be overwhelmingly positive. The point is that the consequences of what we choose to do can slide those immediately involved, those affected, and those who just hear or watch what follows. All matter. Related: Upsurges Bubble Around the Globe but Will it Evolve into Effective Change? So what should an organization or even just an individual choose to do? How should we decide our personal or organizational agendas? Again there is no one right answer nor even a single right way to think about choosing among possibilities. Some people might best do elements of 1 above, or of 2, 3, or 4, or even of a combination of them and might act with one or another set of tactics. One general consideration might be do different paths require more or less time from participants, duration of involvement, scale of commitment, knowledge of circumstances, and past organizing experience. Where does an organization or where do we as individuals sit on the experience/knowledge/available time spectrum? Are we just getting started in social change or are we quite experienced? How much time can we commit? What the hell am I getting at? As choices of sort 1 through 4 and perhaps others too unfold and seek support some projects will especially welcome and benefit from newcomers but will be less good at utilizing the accumulated lessons or longer time commitments that other potential participants have to give. In contrast, other projects may need greater prior experience and time commitments and more effectively utilize it. Surely in coming months everyone who wants to go forward and not backward will face challenging choices. Suppose we ask not what we like the looks of. Not, where will more people who we know and like be involved. Not, what will be most fun or easiest for us. And not even what we think is the most important task to now accomplish. Suppose we or our organizations instead ask where can we help in a sustained way where we can best utilize whatever learned abilities and other knowledge and time we have and also not occupy a spot that someone with less experience, knowledge and time could do just as well and benefit more from? In other words first we might figure out where we are needed and would not be redundant. And then we might consult a list of what seems most important to get done and ask of all the tasks on that list what could we engage with effectively and sustainably, which would be most sensible to help accomplish. That is one approach individuals and organizations could use to decide, though of course to pursue any approach inflexibly could easily do more harm than good. Specifics are crucial. Exceptions matter. But, nonetheless, let’s very briefly reconsider the four avenues of possible activity mentioned earlier in light of the need to slide people positively along the involvement spectrum and the advisability to apportion our energies there. Related: Trump Needs “Good Americans” to Look the Other Way Type one activity is to hold Trump and his sycophants accountable with public investigations, impeachments, and prosecutions. While this is mostly activity for elected officials, others might organize, write and speak about the need for it, or might report on it and urge it. The potentially positive aspect is that the type 1 choices can advance the concept of accountability and reduce prospects of these vile characters doing further damage. But negatively, type 1 pursuits might distract Congress and others from working on positive policies and may highlight bad individuals but not bad institutions. Type one choices may highlight “low-bar” changes to get rid of grotesque criminality but ignore more substantive policy much less structural possibilities. At its worst, type 1 activity might complain about Hegseth having weakened America (which is arguably the only positive accomplishment of Trump’s whole tenure) but not address the perversity of war itself. To highlight to punish criminality might say nothing about what ought to characterize a worthy cabinet member or President while it emphasizes only that a Secretary of War should not be a bigoted, violence-worshipping psychopath and a Secretary of Health and Human Services should not be a pseudo scientific self-seeking anti-health nut. Such work might positively affect some on the involvement spectrum, but it could also bore and make cynical many others. It may be the best that activists can reasonably hope for from some elected officials so it is better than if they do nothing especially if some activists pressure outcomes so as to accentuate positive and diminish negative effects. Still, for the most part this isn’t a path likely to effectively utilize experienced radical energies—with perhaps one possible exception. Unlike dumping the likes of Hegseth, etc., work to remove Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries from Democratic Party leadership, especially if it clearly indicates what it would take for new candidates to be worth supporting, could push beyond castigating personal failings to help define and pursue positive policy and structural gains. Type two activity is to win still bigger ballot box gains in 2028 by working with the Democratic Party as a whole or with particular preferred candidates while opposing others. This could certainly welcome new people into outreach activity while simultaneously preparing to win new gains. It could arouse hope and attention and involve new recruits rather like the midterms did only much more so. But how to do this constructively is another matter. Supposing one’s overall goal is to improve conditions for current victims of injustice at home and abroad, if type 2 activity were to melt into compliant Democratic Party allegiance it could limit positive prospects and be unlikely to permanently shift many people on the involvement spectrum other than, perhaps, toward cynicism. On the other hand, to build support for particular demonstrably progressive candidates and especially to build grassroots mechanisms to inform and pressure such candidates and later office holders to radically address public needs could be part of positively shifting popular commitments and desires. How words and actions communicate, as well as the votes they garner, would matter. Type 3 activity is to organize to win universal free health care, an end to ICE, an end to the Iran war, the Israeli/U.S. genocide terminated, public education restored, sexual and social diversity defended, cancelled departments and programs brought back better, corruption prosecuted, tariff idiocy terminated, price controls enacted, low incomes raised, a national wealth tax with draconian consequences for trying to flee it, and so on. These choices can improve people’s lives especially if they are pursued creatively and not solely as ends but also as means to produce growing desires and then pursue them. They can slide people leftward on the involvement spectrum and elevate reasoned hope. Type 3 activity would then have no negatives unless it’s rhetoric and tactics, were to repel rather than attract public support. Fighting for something good by using words and acts that induce fear of change or that castigate and shame potential new people rather than hear and reach out to them can slide involvement in the wrong direction and also provoke preventable repression, so to carefully avoid such debits matters. Type 4 activity is to build activism and consciousness able to inspire on-going struggle beyond 2028 by developing new workplace, campus, and community organizations and movements, growing existing ones, and especially developing and advocating shared social vision, strategy, and program able to orient future institutional renovation. To try to accomplish all that without simultaneous efforts to grow popular support would ultimately fail to deliver. Then again so would to only slide people along the involvement spectrum without having developed means and aims that growing numbers of motivated people could pursue. Strategy has many facets. Being strategic is necessary to keep momentum building. Related: From the New Left to Trump: Why Movements of the 1960s Failed to Build Lasting Power If the above suggestions have merit, what might DSA, for example, choose to do to slide public consciousness along the involvement spectrum and to prod and pursue sustainable movement growth? Where might DSA-level organization and energy be most effectively applied? Different people will likely see this differently but I would suggest least attention and perhaps even none should go directly to type 1 activity. If needed, some attention should go to type 2 activity while carefully retaining an external independent identity and recognizing that electoral victories in 2028 may not require very much DSA time and creativity supposing massive electoral participation rises from previously less experienced people via effective candidate outreach. In that case, considerable DSA level organization, thought, and organizing might better go to type 3 struggles and especially to type 4 vision, strategy, and organization building. So we have lots of if/then formulations. Can we say anything definitive? Perhaps that while paralysis due to excessive analysis is possible, a shortage of effective analysis pretty much guarantees that we will squander energetic effort in unproductive or even destructive pursuits. To perceive and take account of local contexts and especially wide consequences is an essential part of doing good work. Z Network
